segments.text: Motivation explains why behaviour starts, where it is directed and why it continues. Emotion involves subjective feeling, bodily arousal, expression and cognitive interpretation. In examination answers, motivation answers “why act?” while emotion answers “what is felt and how is it experienced?”

The key is to compare theories rather than memorizing isolated names. Every theory tries to explain the source and direction of behaviour or the relationship among bodily arousal, interpretation and emotional experience.

items.text: Homeostasis

: Homeostasis is the body’s tendency to maintain internal stability. Drive-based explanations propose that biological imbalances can create tension that motivates behaviour aimed at restoring balance.
Biogenic and social motives
: Biogenic motives are tied closely to biological needs such as hunger and thirst. Social motives develop strongly through social experience and may include achievement, affiliation, status or power.
Factors affecting motivation
: Needs, goals, incentives, expectations, past learning, culture and situational opportunities can influence motivation. No single factor explains all human action.
Measuring motivation
: Motivation is often inferred from behaviour, self-report, persistence, choice, performance and sometimes physiological measures. Each method has limitations.
Theories of motivation

: Prepare drive-reduction, incentive, arousal, cognitive/expectancy and humanistic approaches as different ways of explaining motivation. The examiner usually rewards comparison and application more than name-listing.
Emotion and physiological change
: Emotions involve changes in autonomic activity, expression and cognition. Fear, anger, sadness, joy and other emotions may share some physiological features but differ in appraisal and context.
Theories of emotion

: Classic theories differ over whether bodily arousal comes before conscious emotion, occurs alongside it, or is interpreted through cognitive appraisal. A comparison diagram is the easiest way to present them.

segments.text: The following sections develop the compressed source notes into the academic depth needed for first-time understanding and analytical answer writing.

items.text: Initiation
: Motivation helps explain why a behaviour begins. Hunger may initiate food-seeking, while a valued academic goal may initiate study.
Direction
: Motivation also explains choice: among possible behaviours, people select actions that appear capable of meeting needs, goals or incentives.
Persistence
: Motivational processes affect how long effort continues in the face of delay, difficulty or competing goals. Persistence therefore cannot be reduced to one personality trait such as 'willpower'.
Intensity
: Effort can vary in strength. High motivation may increase effort, but extreme arousal can impair performance on complex tasks, so more activation is not always better.
Drive-reduction

: Drive theories begin with physiological imbalance. Need creates an internal drive, behaviour reduces the drive and homeostasis is restored. This fits some biological motives but does not explain curiosity, risk-taking or behaviours pursued without a deficit.
Incentive
: Incentive approaches emphasize attractive or aversive external goals. A behaviour can be motivated because an outcome is expected to be rewarding even when no biological deficit exists.
Arousal

: Arousal approaches propose that people regulate desired levels of stimulation. The relationship between arousal and performance depends on task difficulty and the person, so a single optimum cannot be applied to every situation.
Expectancy-value
: Cognitive approaches emphasize what people expect will happen and how much they value the outcome. A learner may value success but still avoid effort if they believe success is impossible.
Self-determination

: Self-determination theory distinguishes qualities of motivation and emphasizes autonomy, competence and relatedness. External rewards can motivate behaviour, but enduring engagement is stronger when people also experience meaningful internal reasons.
Humanistic
: Maslow's hierarchy drew attention to growth and human needs, but the strict universal ordering of needs has limited empirical support. It is better used as a broad heuristic than as a fixed law.

segments.text: Emotion includes subjective experience, physiological activation, expressive behaviour and cognitive appraisal. These components can influence one another but need not occur in a single rigid sequence. Culture also shapes which emotions are emphasized, how they are labelled and when expression is considered appropriate.

items.text: James-Lange theory

: The classic James-Lange view proposes that perception of bodily changes contributes to the conscious experience of emotion: event -> physiological response -> experienced emotion. The theory highlighted embodiment but is too simple if treated as the whole explanation.
Cannon-Bard theory

: Cannon and Bard argued that emotional experience and physiological arousal can occur in parallel rather than one simply causing the other. This corrected the idea that conscious emotion must wait for bodily feedback.
Two-factor theory

: Schachter and Singer proposed that emotion depends on physiological arousal plus cognitive interpretation of the situation. The approach shows why similar arousal can be experienced differently depending on context.
Appraisal theories
: Appraisal approaches emphasize evaluations of significance, control, responsibility and coping resources. They explain why two people can experience the same event differently.
Self-report
: People can report goals, feelings and perceived motives, but answers may be affected by memory, self-presentation or limited self-awareness.
Behavioural indicators
: Persistence, choices and effort provide useful evidence, but the same behaviour can arise from different motives. Interpretation therefore requires context.
Physiological indicators
: Heart rate, skin conductance and hormonal measures can index arousal, but no single measure uniquely identifies a specific emotion.
Practical application

: In education and organizations, motivation is strengthened by combining clear goals, credible feedback, appropriate challenge, fair incentives and opportunities for autonomy rather than assuming one reward will work equally for everyone.

Use hunger for a biological motive and achievement for a social motive.
Draw the sequence proposed by James-Lange, Cannon-Bard and two-factor approaches in simple arrows.
Prepare one paragraph on how cognition and culture can shape emotional experience.

rows: Avoid this error Do not present motivation as only “willpower.” Behaviour is influenced by needs, incentives, expectations, learning and context.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Define motivation and emotion separately, explain motives and homeostasis, compare motivation theories, then explain emotional components and compare major emotion theories with a small flow diagram.
• Homeostasis explains some biological motivation but not all human motives.
• Social motives are influenced by learning and culture.
• Emotion includes bodily, cognitive and experiential components.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
